sources.title: Video Surveillance in Public Areas Procedure
sources.excerpt: anch DATE: August 1, 2002 TITLE: VIDEO SURVEILLANCE IN PUBLIC AREAS Directive Statement: The City of Edmonton recognizes the need to balance an individual’s right to protection of privacy against the city’s duty to promote a safe environment for all citizens, and to protect city property. This directive is intended to assist departments in deciding whether collection of personal information by means of a surveillance camera is both lawful and justifiable, and if so, in understanding how privacy protection measures can be built into the use of a surveillance system. It is recognized that each department has unique needs and practices. While these requirements will remain, it is necessary to standardize city procedures in order that all citizens have an expectation of consistency, regardless where the equipment is installed. The purpose of this policy is to: Develop a surveillance system policy that complies with the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act. Ensure consistency of corporate surveillance measures. These guidelines do not apply to covert or overt surveillance cameras being used as a case-specific investigation tool for law enforcement purposes or in contemplation of litigation. They are also not intended to apply to workplace surveillance systems installed to conduct surveillance of employees. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURE DIRECTIVE A1435 NUMBER: AUTHORITY: City Manager EFFECTIVE DATE: August 1, 2002 TITLE:

followupSources.excerpt: e Jasper Pop-Up Village is a temporary marketplace for businesses affected by the 2024 wildfire. It gives them a place to operate while their permanent locations are being rebuilt. The Village offers lots with power and water for small modular units, trailers, or shipping containers. This helps businesses reopen quickly, keep staff working, and serve the community. Businesses that have participated include: Vicious Cycles Coco's Cafe Rockaboo Mountain Adventures Lynn's Place Andaaz Indian Cuisine Maligne Raft Tours Jasper Motorcycle Tours - call 780-931-6100 for reservations ELM Contemporary Considering Joining the Jasper Pop-Up Village? If your business was displaced by the 2024 wildfire and you are still navigating rebuild timelines or lease uncertainty, the Jasper Pop-Up Village may provide a practical path forward. The Pop-Up Village is designed to help eligible businesses continue operating, retain staff, and remain visible in the community while permanent locations are rebuilt. If you meet the eligibility criteria (see below), we encourage you to explore participation and connect with us to discuss whether the Pop-Up Village is the right fit for your business recovery journey

sources.excerpt: CONSOLIDATED November 9, 2023 CONSOLIDATED FOR CONVENIENCE PURPOSES OF BYLAW: 3930 CITY OF CAMPBELL RIVER PROVINCE OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BYLAW NO. 3498 A BYLAW OF THE CITY OF CAMPBELL RIVER TO ESTABLISH FEES FOR SERVICES PROVIDED IN RESPONSE TO A FALSE ALARM. The Council of the City of Campbell River, in open meeting assembled, enacts as follows: 1. TITLE This Bylaw may be cited for all purposes as “False Alarm Fees Bylaw No. 3498, 2013”. 2. DEFINITIONS In this Bylaw, unless the context otherwise requires: “Alarm Business” means a person who is engaged in the business of monitoring alarm systems and reporting the occurrence of alarms to the Police and the Fire Department. “City” means the City of Campbell River. "False Alarm" means the activation of a Fire Alarm System or a Security Alarm System resulting in the direct or indirect notification to the Fire Department or Police for which Fire Department or Police services are provided on behalf of the City and the providers of the service do not find any unauthorized entry or commission of an unlawful act or any evidence of fire, fire damage or smoke in relation to the building, structure, residence or facility, or where there has been no emergency situation. False Alarm incidents also include but are not limited to: i) The testing of an alarm which results in a Fire Department or Police response; ii) An alarm actually or apparently activated by mechanical failure, malfunction or faulty equipment; iii) An alarm activated by user error; iv) An alarm reporting an attempted or completed criminal offence or an emergency situation occurring on or in relation to the premises in which the alarm system is installed where no evidence exists or where no such event took place. “Fire Alarm System” means a device or devices installed on

priorDecision.heading: Separate equipment faults from reportable emergencies
priorDecision.body: Campbell River’s False Alarm Fees Bylaw No. 3498 defines false alarms to include testing that causes a response, malfunction and user error, and distinguishes security alarm systems from fire systems. This is municipal response regulation, not a specification for every detector. Start the intrusion assessment with an activation history, detector locations and the people who arm the premises. Investigate repeated mechanical faults separately from training issues, then record corrective action and a controlled test procedure. Confirm the current bylaw and amendments before relying on the convenience consolidation. Do not infer that an activation will receive a particular police response.

sources.excerpt: District of Chetwynd BYLAW NO. 1135 A BYLAW TO PROVIDE FOR THE REGULATION OF FIRE AND SECURITY ALARM SYSTEMS WHEREAS Part 3, Division 10 of the Community Charter authorizes a local government to regulate, prohibit and impose requirements in relation to the protection of persons and property; AND WHEREAS section 196 of the Community Charter authorizes a local government to impose fees for False Alarms originating from fire and security Alarm Systems; AND WHEREAS such False Alarms require emergency responses from the Fire Department and/or Police and such unnecessary emergency responses pose a threat to the safety of fire fighters, Police and members of the public by creating unnecessary hazards and, in addition, fire and Police response to a False Alarm may result in a delayed response to a true emergency; AND WHEREAS excessive numbers of False Alarms are being permitted to occur by the Owners or users of fire and security Alarm Systems; AND WHEREAS the Council of the District of Chetwynd deems it expedient to provide for regulations and prohibitions regarding emergency services in response to False Alarms; AND WHEREAS section 258(1)(b) of the Charter permits the recovery of unpaid fees for fees that are to be paid by the Owner of real property for services in response to a False Alarm in the same manner as taxes deemed in arrears; NOW THEREFORE the Council of the District of Chetwynd in open meeting assembled enacts as follows: 1. CITATION This bylaw may be cited as "District of Chetwynd False Alarm Bylaw No. 1135, 2021." 2. DEFINITIONS In this bylaw the following definitions shall apply: "Activate" or “Activation” means the triggering of an Alarm System, either intentional or accidental, which results in an alarm response including, but not limited to, an audible siren

priorDecision.heading: Distinguish alarm activation from evidence of an emergency
priorDecision.body: Chetwynd’s False Alarm Bylaw No. 1135, 2021 regulates fire and security alarm systems and describes activation broadly, including audible signals, visual displays, monitoring alerts and dispatch. For an intrusion project, identify which outputs the panel produces and how each reaches the responsible person before changing programming. Review accidental activations alongside equipment faults and arrange testing so it does not unnecessarily trigger emergency attendance. The document supplies a District regulatory context, not a guarantee of response or a requirement for every premises to buy the same equipment. Confirm amendments and the applicable alarm category before using the bylaw in a final operating procedure.

By using this website, you agree to our use of cookies as explained in our Privacy Policy . Agree Bylaws and Policies Section Menu Find more information on the City of Dawson Creek's bylaws and policies . Bylaws explained Bylaws are laws created by the City and the City Bylaw Officers enforce the bylaws. Bylaws need three readings before consideration of adoption. Most bylaws receive the first three readings at one meeting, and then adoption is considered at the following meeting. There are different requirements for zoning and OCP bylaws. The public is encouraged to provide input. Example of a Bylaw: The Parking Bylaw No. 4214 . This provides Council with the authority, by bylaw, to regulate parking within the City limits and remove vehicles that are in contravention of this bylaw. Search all bylaws Information about our bylaws Each bylaw has a title and a number, for example, Noise Bylaw 3873. Each amendment to the bylaw also has a number but if you want to see the bylaw with all its amendments incorporated, look for the Consolidated Bylaw. Consolidated bylaws - For convenience, the most used bylaws have been consolidated. In a consolidated bylaw, we updated the original bylaw (or "parent" bylaw) to include all the amendments to that bylaw. Individual bylaws - Each individual bylaw has an unique number. An individual bylaw may be a "parent" bylaw or it may be an amending bylaw. If you need an Official Copy of a bylaw, contact the Corporate Officer by email . sources.excerpt: Township bolstering security at municipal facilities | Corporation of the Township of Esquimalt Skip to main content Township bolstering security at municipal facilities February 3, 2020 Type(s) News Visitors to Esquimalt facilities may observe the addition of cameras in some public spaces in the next week. The cameras will be there to add an additional layer of safety and security for Township staff, clients, visitors, facilities and properties. The Township will be following the rules set out in the Freedom of Information and Personal Privacy Act (FIPPA) and will balance the need to protect municipal assets with individuals’ want of privacy. Signage will indicate where the cameras are located. Records are retained for public safety or security, criminal investigations, evidentiary purposes, as otherwise required by law, or disclosed to a request for access to records under FIPPA; however the Township does not retain the original or a copy of any record for longer than 30 days unless it is flagged for a longer retention. Any records that are accessed or disclosed under FIPPA shall be securely retained by the Township for the required period in accordance with the Township’s Records Management Policy. Any questions about the collection of personal information or requests for access to records may be directed to the Corporate Officer, Township of Esquimalt, 1229 Esquimalt Road, Esquimalt, BC V9A 3P1, or by telephone at 250-414-7135. More information about privacy and video recording can be found at Esquimalt.ca/privacy . Category Esquimalt News
sources.scope: February 3, 2020 municipal-facility camera announcement; historical municipal example, not a private-business retention rule.

priorDecision.heading: Treat the Township retention practice as a civic example
priorDecision.body: Esquimalt’s February 2020 announcement describes adding cameras in municipal public spaces, posting signage and normally retaining recordings for no longer than 30 days unless flagged for longer retention. The announcement concerns Township facilities and is a historical operational example, not a retention requirement for another owner. A camera planning brief should distinguish ordinary overwriting from incident preservation, name the person who can authorize access and show where notices will be visible. Check the actual property’s privacy obligations before adopting a retention period. The announcement does not verify current equipment condition, coverage or live monitoring arrangements.

sources.excerpt: File No. 0340-50 Administration PRIVACY MANAGEMENT POLICY Council Policy No. 140/24 1 PURPOSE To establish guidelines for the collection, use, disclosure, storage, and retention of personal information by the City of Fort St. John (the “City”) and to ensure personal information in the custody or under the control of the City is protected. To ensure the City, as a public body, manages personal information in accordance with the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, RSBC 1996, c 165 (“FIPPA”). 2 SCOPE This Policy applies to all employees, elected officials, and volunteers of the City. The privacy obligations of the City equally apply and flow down to all service providers where collection, use, disclosure, security, and access to personal information may be required while performing services under contract to the City. FIPPA and the regulations under it prevail over this policy. 3 POLICY STATEMENT The City is subject to FIPPA and is committed to the responsible management of personal and confidential information within the City’s custody and control. This Policy is established in accordance with the City’s Freedom of Information Bylaw, the “FOI Bylaw”. 4 INTERPRETATION In this Policy: “contact information” is information to enable an individual at a place of business to be contacted, including the name, position name or title, business telephone number, business address, business e-mail, or business fax number of the individual. Council Resolution No. 50/24 Effective: February 26, 2024 Supersedes Council Resolution No. 48/19 Page: 1 of 13 File No. 0340-50 Administration PRIVACY MANAGEMENT POLICY Council Policy No. 140/24 “day” does not include Saturday, Sunday or holidays. “employee” means a person who is employed by the City, an elected official of the Ci
sources.scope: Municipal employees, elected officials, volunteers and contracted service providers handling City personal information; not a general business cyber standard.

sources.excerpt: Alertable Emergency Alerts - Hope, BC Skip to main content Search Local Weather Air Quality Search Home A A A Alertable Emergency Alerts Staying informed is one of the most important things you can do before, during, and after an emergency. The District of Hope uses Alertable , a free public alerting system that provides real-time notifications about emergencies, public safety incidents, and important community information. Alertable helps residents receive timely updates so they can make informed decisions and take appropriate action when needed. What is Alertable? Alertable is a multi-platform notification system that delivers alerts directly to your preferred devices, including: Smartphones and tablets Computers and web browsers Smart speakers Email notifications Users can customize the locations and types of alerts they wish to receive, ensuring they stay informed about events that matter most to them. Types of Alerts Alertable may be used to provide notifications about: Wildfires Evacuation Alerts and Evacuation Orders Flooding and severe weather Road closures and transportation disruptions Public safety incidents Emergency Management updates Other important community notifications Why Sign Up? sources.title: False Alarms
sources.excerpt: False Alarms | City of Kamloops Skip to main content Skip to main menu Skip to footer Search Related Contacts Related Pages Related Pages Related Links Related Links Related Documents Related Documents Related News Related News Share page Related Contacts Related Pages Related Pages Related Links Related Links Related Documents Related Documents Related News Related News Share page False Alarms Reducing Excessive False Alarms in Kamloops Security alarm systems play an important role in protecting homes and businesses. However, when alarm systems are activated accidentally or due to equipment issues, police resources are diverted away from higher-priority policing needs. The City of Kamloops Security Alarm System Bylaw helps reduce unnecessary police responses by establishing responsibilities, service fees, and fines related to false alarms. The bylaw applies to both residential and commercial security alarm systems that result in RCMP attendance. Security Alarm System Bylaw No. 10-43 What is a false alarm? A false alarm is the activation of an alarm system that results in an RCMP response when no evidence of unauthorized entry, an unlawful act, or an emergency is found. Common causes of false alarm activation include, but are not limited to: testing of the alarm system without prior notice to the RCMP and the monitoring company user error, mechanical failure, malfunction, or faulty equipment atmospheric conditions, excessive vibration, power failure, or trigger sensitivity A false alarm does not include alarm activations resulting from proven criminal activity, attempted break-ins, or other legitimate emergencies. Why are false alarms concerning? False alarms consume valuable police resources and taxpayer dollars. In 2025, the RCMP responded to approximately 840 alarm-r
sources.scope: Municipal guidance for residential and commercial security alarms resulting in RCMP attendance; page references Bylaw 10-43, 2026.

priorDecision.heading: Build maintenance and contact review into alarm handover
priorDecision.body: Kamloops’ False Alarms page describes security alarms that result in RCMP attendance and identifies testing without notice, equipment faults and user error among causes of unwanted responses. Its scope includes residential and commercial security systems, rather than all building alarm technologies. Review maintenance records and the monitoring company’s contact information before changing detectors or panel programming. Record who informs the monitoring company before tests and who can attend the premises. The page references the 2026 Security Alarm System Bylaw; confirm its applicable commencement and current provisions for the project rather than relying on an older alarm process or assuming police attendance is guaranteed.
priorDecision.reason: Direct fetched official text supports this limited planning context, not service coverage or approval.
priorDecision.independentReviewReason: Excerpt supports residential/commercial security alarms resulting in RCMP attendance and the stated false-alarm causes. Full page confirms contact and training guidance and September 1, 2026 fee commencement. Precision warning: the visible 2026 date identifies the fee schedule, not necessarily the enactment year of Bylaw 10-43; do not publish a 2026 bylaw-year attribution without the actual instrument. The limited alarm-operation candidate remains usable; current legal commencement and attendance must not be assumed.

sources.title: Smoke Alarm Regulations
sources.excerpt: Smoke Alarm Regulations | City of Kimberley Skip to main content Image Smoke Alarm Regulations Dated: July 16, 2012 Ministry of Justice (Revised December 13, 2013) Emergency Management BC Smoke Alarm Bulletin British Columbia’s fire statistics reveal a strong link between working smoke alarms and reduced fatalities from residential structure fires. Numerous evaluations have been conducted by the Fire Service using decades of data and the results are consistent. Working smoke alarms save lives. Statistics show that smoke alarms help save lives, reduce fire related injuries, reduce the spread of fires, and reduce the damage caused by fire. International studies show that your chances of dying in a home fire may be reduced by 5o percent if a working smoke alarm is present in your home. Most fire deaths happen in homes as a result of people breathing smoke and toxic fumes while they are asleep. Smoke alarms are an effective early warning device that can awaken sleeping occupants and help provide time to safely exit the building. Smoke alarms are mandatory in all dwellings (homes and sleeping rooms). Under the British Columbia Fire Code all homes, and all sleeping rooms within boarding and lodging houses, hotels and recreational cabins, are required to be protected by smoke alarms. Dwelling units constructed before the British Columbia Building Code required smoke alarms in 1979 are also required to have a smoke alarm. Smoke alarms are permitted to be battery operated in a dwelling unit constructed before the March 31, 1979 British Columbia Building Code inception date or in a building which is not supplied with electrical power. Dwelling units constructed after the 1979 building code changes require the smoke alarms to be permanently wired to the home’s electrical system an

sources.title: Video Surveillance of Civic Property Policy COU-223
sources.excerpt: PURPOSE: To establish guidelines for the use of video surveillance to enhance the security and safety of persons, properties, things, and activities that are in or near facilities, infrastructure or on properties owned or occupied by the City of Nanaimo and used for public civic purposes. DEFINITIONS: Personal Information Means recorded information about an identifiable individual other than business contact information Privacy Impact Means a process which assists organizations in identifying and managing the Assessment (PIA) privacy risks arising from new projects, initiatives, systems, or processes. PIAs must be approved by the Freedom of Information Head (FOI Head) SCOPE: This Policy applies to any video surveillance system operated by or for the City of Nanaimo that collects personal information in any form. This Policy does not apply to video surveillance conducted by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), who are subject to the Privacy Act (Canada). POLICY: 1.0 PRINCIPLES 1.1 As an owner of significant public assets that represent a large investment of public money, the City of Nanaimo makes use of video surveillance systems to better monitor and protect the security of its people, assets and property. 1.2 The City acknowledges that the use of video surveillance may, in some circumstances, represent a potential intrusion into personal privacy and does not wish to impair personal privacy any more than is warranted to provide necessary and reasonable protection of its property against crimes such as vandalism, theft, damage and destruction. Video surveillance recordings can be used by the City for an investigation and as evidence in any civil proceedings. 1.3 Video surveillance systems will be installed if, in the opinion of the City of Nanaimo, there is a risk t
sources.scope: City-operated or contracted civic surveillance; expressly excludes RCMP surveillance.

priorDecision.heading: Keep civic-camera authority and privacy assessment together
priorDecision.body: Nanaimo’s Video Surveillance of Civic Property Policy applies to systems operated by or for the City that collect personal information and expressly excludes RCMP surveillance. It identifies privacy impact assessment approval as part of its governance framework. For work on a civic property, establish the responsible City decision maker and the approved purpose before expanding a camera view. Compare new coverage, recording access and storage arrangements with the assessment rather than treating a hardware replacement as automatically equivalent. For a private building, this is a scoped municipal governance example only; its provisions do not automatically become that owner’s privacy policy or establish a mandatory camera layout.

sources.title: Parking Enforcement Methods
sources.excerpt: Parking Enforcement Methods | City of New Westminster Transportation Planning Travel in New Westminster Parking & Towing Parking Pay a Parking Ticket Parking Permits Parking Payment Methods Pay Stations and Meters Passport Mobile Parking App Designated Disabled On-Street Parking Frequently Asked Questions Towing Street Occupancy Permit Speed Humps Trucks Railways Roadworks & Construction Projects Q to Q Ferry Parking Enforcement Methods Street use enforcement and parking officers monitor and enforce sections with the Street and Traffic Bylaw . Officers respond to Calls for Service from the public through multiple reporting streams. Officers monitor street use and parking through a variety of methods, some of which include, electronic parking reports, Licence Plate Recognition (LPR), and conventional foot patrols. License Plate Recognition System (LPR) What is LPR? The LPR is a license plate recognition application whereby vehicles observed by cameras taking pictures, have their license plates read, recorded and checked against a pre-loaded data base using pattern recognition software. Peace officers will review and assess all information, correcting for system errors, and controlling the issuing of violation notices. The system is located in either marked City vehicles, which have four (4) cameras mounted on the vehicle, two facing forward and one to each side. The system is run on a laptop mounted in the patrol vehicle with communication using encrypted cellular technology with the City network in real time, or as a static camera at the entrance to the parkade. Mobile Version The Parking Services branch runs two vehicles equipped with LPR camera. These vehicles are linked in real time with the City’s system which allows them to automatically verify payment at digital m

priorDecision.heading: Separate parking recognition data from ordinary surveillance footage
priorDecision.body: New Westminster describes licence-plate recognition for municipal parking enforcement, including officer review and deletion of collected data after 72 hours unless transferred into ticketing systems because an offence occurred. This is a parking enforcement application, not a general CCTV retention policy. A similar planning discussion should distinguish transient recognition data, reviewed violations and exported evidence as separate records. Identify who checks recognition errors and how exceptions to ordinary deletion are documented. Do not copy the parking retention period into a business camera system without an independent privacy review. The page also does not establish that unrelated cameras should use automated recognition or real-time network links.

No general retention, mandatory analytics or unrelated real-time network requirement follows.

sources.excerpt: Parking Enforcement Methods | City of New Westminster Transportation Planning Travel in New Westminster Parking & Towing Parking Pay a Parking Ticket Parking Permits Parking Payment Methods Pay Stations and Meters Passport Mobile Parking App Designated Disabled On-Street Parking Frequently Asked Questions Towing Street Occupancy Permit Speed Humps Trucks Railways Roadworks & Construction Projects Q to Q Ferry Parking Enforcement Methods Street use enforcement and parking officers monitor and enforce sections with the Street and Traffic Bylaw . Officers respond to Calls for Service from the public through multiple reporting streams. Officers monitor street use and parking through a variety of methods, some of which include, electronic parking reports, Licence Plate Recognition (LPR), and conventional foot patrols. License Plate Recognition System (LPR) What is LPR? The LPR is a license plate recognition application whereby vehicles observed by cameras taking pictures, have their license plates read, recorded and checked against a pre-loaded data base using pattern recognition software. Peace officers will review and assess all information, correcting for system errors, and controlling the issuing of violation notices. The system is located in either marked City vehicles, which have four (4) cameras mounted on the vehicle, two facing forward and one to each side. The system is run on a laptop mounted in the patrol vehicle with communication using encrypted cellular technology with the City network in real time, or as a static camera at the entrance to the parkade. Mobile Version The Parking Services branch runs two vehicles equipped with LPR camera. These vehicles are linked in real time with the City’s system which allows them to automatically verify payment at digital m

cctv.body: New Westminster describes licence-plate recognition for municipal parking enforcement, including officer review and deletion of collected data after 72 hours unless transferred into ticketing systems because an offence occurred. This is a parking enforcement application, not a general CCTV retention policy. Identify who checks recognition errors and how exceptions to ordinary deletion are documented. Do not copy the parking retention period into a business camera system without an independent privacy review. priorDecision.heading: Check burglar-alarm exclusions before applying the bylaw
priorDecision.body: Oak Bay’s Burglar Alarm Bylaw No. 3832 addresses unwanted security-alarm responses and defines an alarm business as monitoring systems and reporting alarms to police. Its alarm-system definition includes exclusions, including devices installed in motor vehicles. Use those distinctions to classify the actual installation before building an operating checklist. Record detection zones, audible or transmitted outputs, user training and recurring activation causes so maintenance work addresses the identified failure rather than merely resetting the panel. The fetched document is an older amended bylaw, so confirm current provisions with the District. It is not evidence that every local alarm has identical reporting obligations or receives police attendance.

intrusion.heading: Check burglar-alarm exclusions before applying the bylaw
intrusion.body: Oak Bay’s Burglar Alarm Bylaw No. 3832 addresses unwanted security-alarm responses and defines an alarm business as monitoring systems and reporting alarms to police. Its alarm-system definition includes exclusions, including devices installed in motor vehicles. Use those distinctions to classify the actual installation before building an operating checklist. Record detection zones, audible or transmitted outputs, user training and recurring activation causes so maintenance work addresses the identified failure rather than merely resetting the panel. The fetched document is an older amended bylaw, so confirm current provisions with the District. It is not evidence that every local alarm has identical reporting obligations or receives police attendance.

intrusion.independentReviewReason: Excerpt supports false-alarm purpose, alarm businesses reporting to police and motor-vehicle exclusion. It also excludes devices not perceptible outside the premises: retain the complete definition when determining applicability. Zone lists, training and maintenance suggestions are generic professional advice rather than local obligations. Older amended bylaw supports a scoped historical candidate, not current-law assurance.

sources.excerpt: City partners with DPA to enhance downtown safety | City of Penticton Skip to main content Alerts City partners with DPA to enhance downtown safety October 14, 2021 News Release Penticton City Council has agreed to immediately move ahead with a crime deterrent pilot project brought forward by the Downtown Penticton Association (DPA) and presented to Council on October 5, 2021 by Councillor Watt as a 2022 budget ‘Notice of Motion’. Supporting the strategic priority of Community Safety, Council has directed staff to provide the DPA with a $40,000 grant to fund the project costs associated with installing downtown surveillance cameras on commercial properties. Located in three to five high-crime locations, and featuring signage, two-way voice notifications and strobe lights, each camera will be monitored from 9pm to 9am with the operator, if needed, advising those trespassing or acting irresponsibly to move on or, if needed, dispatching a response from either Bylaw or the RCMP. “By way of this pilot project, businesses and residents in the downtown will gain a better sense of security knowing that our Bylaw and RCMP are responding to issues that are happening, versus issues that have happened,” said Penticton Mayor, John Vassilaki. “Overall, the situation downtown is challenging, and while there’s no single solution for addressing the deliberate disorder we witness, I’m pleased to see proactive organizations like the DPA helping the situation by coming forward to Council with ideas that we can introduce now to deter poor behavior and respond to crime.” “In keeping with City Council’s focus on security, we created this program to fit within the scope of the Community Safety Strategic Priority. Terms of Service The CCTV Registry allows you to proactively participate in the enhancement of your community’s public safety by confidentially and voluntarily registering your surveillance recording camera(s) with the City of Prince George. By registering your surveillance equipment, you will be helping law enforcement quickly identify the location and owners of potential sources of video evidence, decreasing time, effort, and cost of an incident investigation. By voluntarily registering your camera equipment with the City of Prince George, you acknowledge and agree to the following: You are registering only those cameras that you own and manage. sources.scope: Voluntary owner-managed camera registry; police contact owners for potential evidence.

priorDecision.heading: Prepare owner-controlled footage retrieval before registry participation
priorDecision.body: Prince George’s CCTV Registry Program is voluntary and requires participants to register cameras they own and manage. Its terms describe confidential handling of contact and camera-location information so law enforcement can identify potential recorded evidence and contact the owner. For a participating property, verify the accountable contact, camera inventory and a practical method for finding and exporting relevant footage. Keep registry details accurate when ownership or equipment changes, and establish a separate process for reviewing requests. Registration is not permission for unrestricted live police access and does not replace the owner’s privacy assessment. The programme also does not establish that a recording will exist when investigators request it.

sources.title: Video Surveillance Policy CCR-6
sources.excerpt: Video Surveillance Policy – CCR-6 Effective: June 4, 2019 Authorized By: Council Resolution: 19-15-283 Replaces: April 26, 2010, March 27, 2018 Scope The City of Quesnel in its’ commitment to public safety has initiated a program to deter and prevent nuisance, mischief, theft and vandalism in, on or near property and facilities owned or occupied by the City and to support law enforcement, through the use of video surveillance cameras at certain locations of our open public areas. Safeguards will be implemented to protect the privacy of our citizens while at the same time providing enhanced safety in the use and enjoyment of the public space in our community. The program is intended to be consistent with the Privacy Act of Canada and the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act of British Columbia. DEFINITIONS “Acts” mean the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, RSBC 1996, c. 165 and the Privacy Act of Canada. “FOI Head” means the person or persons designated to act on behalf of the City for the purposes of the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act and to carry out the powers, duties and functions of the head under the Act. “Guidelines” mean the “Guidelines for the Use of Video Surveillance of Public Places by Police and Law Enforcement Authorities” published by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, or similar guidelines published by the Information and Privacy Commissioner of British Columbia, both as may be amended or replaced from time to time. “Personal Information” means recorded information about an identifiable individual as defined under the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act. “Open Public Space” means the grounds of any real property, or portions of real property, owned or subject to a rig
sources.scope: June 4, 2019 municipal public-space/civic-property surveillance policy, not a private-premises rule.

priorDecision.heading: Define the civic public-space purpose before extending a view
priorDecision.body: Quesnel’s Video Surveillance Policy CCR-6 describes cameras at certain open public areas in or near City-owned or occupied property to deter nuisance, mischief, theft and vandalism while protecting privacy. This is a municipal programme with a defined public-space scope, not a rule requiring cameras at every local business. For a civic expansion, map the proposed view against the documented incident and identify unnecessary neighbouring capture before selecting lenses or positions. Assign responsibility for approval, recording access and incident preservation in the project brief. Confirm whether the June 2019 policy has later amendments. Its stated purpose does not prove present camera coverage or justify unrelated analytics.

Safeguards will be implemented to protect the privacy of our citizens while at the same time providing enhanced safety in the use and enjoyment of the public space in our community. The program is intended to be consistent with the Privacy Act of Canada and the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act of British Columbia. DEFINITIONS “Acts” mean the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, RSBC 1996, c. 165 and the Privacy Act of Canada. “FOI Head” means the person or persons designated to act on behalf of the City for the purposes of the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act and to carry out the powers, duties and functions of the head under the Act. “Guidelines” mean the “Guidelines for the Use of Video Surveillance of Public Places by Police and Law Enforcement Authorities” published by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, or similar guidelines published by the Information and Privacy Commissioner of British Columbia, both as may be amended or replaced from time to time. “Personal Information” means recorded information about an identifiable individual as defined under the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act. “Open Public Space” means the grounds of any real property, or portions of real property, owned or subject to a rig

cctv.heading: Define the civic public-space purpose before extending a view
cctv.body: Quesnel’s Video Surveillance Policy CCR-6 describes cameras at certain open public areas in or near City-owned or occupied property to deter nuisance, mischief, theft and vandalism while protecting privacy. This is a municipal programme with a defined public-space scope, not a rule requiring cameras at every local business. For a civic expansion, map the proposed view against the documented incident and identify unnecessary neighbouring capture before selecting lenses or positions. Assign responsibility for approval, recording access and incident preservation in the project brief. Confirm whether the June 2019 policy has later amendments. Its stated purpose does not prove present camera coverage or justify unrelated analytics.

No current inventory or analytics justification established.

sources.excerpt: Cybersecurity & Email Safety - City of Richmond, BC Skip to main content Cybersecurity & Email Safety The City of Richmond, like many organizations, can be a target for cybercrime. We have experienced instances of cybercrime over the past few months and continue to work to prevent such attacks and protect the information and online safety of our customers and staff. We are aware that some fraudulent email messages have been circulating claiming to be from City staff, municipal officials, and Gateway Theatre staff. When the City discovered the intrusion into the email system in June 2023, it took immediate steps to mitigate the risk of impact and remediate the attack by engaging a team of cybersecurity experts to contain and investigate the incident, in accordance with industry best practices. There is no indication any outside party has accessed the City’s financial or human resources data, or any other enterprise systems or databases. City operations were not impacted and business continues as normal. However, in the interest of transparency, we want people to know that fraudulent emails continue to circulate. The following provides important information about the City's ongoing cybersecurity initiatives and how to remain safe in an online environment. What has the City of Richmond done? The City of Richmond engaged cybersecurity experts in June 2023 to investigate, contain and remediate the incident that occurred at that time. The City also placed a public warning regarding fraudulent e-mails on its website, and social media channels. Local media was also advised of the situation. This criminal activity was reported to the RCMP and to the Office of the Information & Privacy Commissioner for British Columbia. Fraudulent email messages often contain a fake PDF file atta

priorDecision.heading: Use the municipal email incident to plan independent verification
priorDecision.body: Richmond’s Cybersecurity & Email Safety page describes fraudulent messages impersonating City or theatre staff following a June 2023 email-system intrusion and explains that specialists were engaged to contain and investigate the incident. The source concerns Richmond, British Columbia municipal communications, not another municipality with the same name. For an organization receiving official-looking messages, define an independent verification route before staff open unexpected attachments or act on changed instructions. Assign reporting and containment responsibilities and preserve relevant message details for investigation. This is a local incident and awareness example, not a published enterprise security architecture, a certification claim or evidence that another organization has suffered the same compromise.
priorDecision.reason: Direct fetched official text supports this limited planning context, not service coverage or approval.

This is service-specific cyber incident/awareness evidence rather than generic emergency-preparedness padding. Independent verification, reporting and evidence-preservation recommendations are editorial advice, not source-proven local enterprise controls. No certification, security architecture or other organizations compromise can be inferred.

sources.title: Video Surveillance Policy
sources.excerpt: POLICY OBJECTIVES: The Video Surveillance Policy aims to: 1. improve and maintain the personal safety of our staff members and citizens by deterring criminal conduct in regards to harassment, assault, thefts or vandalism; 2. assist with the continued integrity, public confidence, security and protection of any or all municipal properties and assets; 3. minimize impacts on personal privacy by reserving the use of any video surveillance technology for legitimate law enforcement purposes; 4. confirm video surveillance equipment is restricted so it cannot be adjusted or manipulated by anyone to overlook spaces that are not intended to be covered by the video surveillance system, 5. ensure applications of video surveillance in City of Rossland facilities and operations are authorized and are compliant with the British Columbia Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FOIPPA). POLICY BACKGROUND/SCOPE: Closed Circuit Video Surveillance (CCTV) is used to serve as a deterrent with respect to criminal activity and ensure proper conduct is administered in relation to City staff members, customers and assets. The City recognizes that any video surveillance technology has a high potential for impacting general individual expectations to privacy and does not wish to breech personal privacy any more than is warranted to provide reasonable protection to City related property. However, the City of Rossland also recognizes the need to strike a balance between an individual’s right to be free from invasion of privacy and the City’s duty to promote a safe environment which protects the security of its staff members, citizens, municipal resources and property. DEFINITIONS: There are no specific terms that need to be defined to understand this policy. Video Surveillance Page 1 o

priorDecision.heading: Prevent camera adjustment from expanding an authorized view
priorDecision.body: Rossland’s Video Surveillance Policy explicitly seeks to restrict equipment so it cannot be manipulated to overlook spaces not intended for coverage. Its scope concerns City facilities and operations and balances asset protection with personal privacy. A municipal camera design should therefore document the intended scene, mounting constraints and who can change orientation or configuration. Include a check after servicing so a repaired or replaced unit does not silently capture additional space. For a private property this is a scoped governance example, not a binding installation standard. Confirm the applicable current policy and approvals; the policy’s objectives do not establish present camera locations or continuous operator observation.

The OCC may provide a General Broadcast without dispatching a police unit when the alarm monitoring company reports an alarm, but has not made attempts to contact property representatives and there are no other extenuating circumstances. 4.3. For the purposes of this policy, a Nuisance Alarm is considered an audible security system that activates three (3) or more false alarms within a twenty-four (24) hour period; or a security alarm system that when activated emits a continuous and/or intermittent audible sound for a period greater than five minutes after the activation. sources.excerpt: Video Monitoring Cameras | City of Vernon Skip to main content Skip to main menu Skip to footer Grey menus Share Video Monitoring Cameras Introduction This webpage is intended to provide information about the video monitoring cameras that are used for safety and security purposes in the City of Vernon under the authority of the City of Vernon’s Video Monitoring Policy . FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS What is the purpose of the Video Monitoring Policy? The Video Monitoring Policy promotes certainty and predictability by creating specific rules around the installation and use of cameras by the City of Vernon, and providing for meaningful oversight of compliance with these rules. This ensures the City complies with its legal obligations to protect privacy when it uses cameras, and aligns the City of Vernon with other Local Governments and Public Institutions that already have policies or guidelines governing camera use. The Video Monitoring Policy The Video Monitoring Policy was developed by Senior Managers and reviewed and approved by the Chief Administrative Officer. Many other local governments and public institutions were contacted and their respective policies and procedures were reviewed and discussed in order to determine best practices. The policy and the program was implemented due to ongoing public requests to improve safety and security in certain areas of the City. The location of the video monitoring systems were chosen due to documented incidents of concern to our citizens. The Video Monitoring Policy promotes certainty and predictability by creating specific rules around the installation and use of cameras by the City of Vernon, and providing for meaningful oversight of compliance with these rules. priorDecision.body: Vernon’s Video Monitoring Cameras FAQ says locations were chosen because of documented incidents and describes rules for installation, use and meaningful oversight under the City’s policy. This is municipal camera governance rather than approval for private surveillance. For a civic proposal, assemble the incident record and explain why the intended camera view addresses that concern before selecting equipment. Record the decision maker, permitted uses and a review point to check whether coverage remains justified. For another property owner, use the example only to structure questions about necessity and accountability. The FAQ does not establish a universal retention period, a guaranteed deterrent effect or permission for unrelated monitoring.

The Video Monitoring Policy The Video Monitoring Policy was developed by Senior Managers and reviewed and approved by the Chief Administrative Officer. Many other local governments and public institutions were contacted and their respective policies and procedures were reviewed and discussed in order to determine best practices. The policy and the program was implemented due to ongoing public requests to improve safety and security in certain areas of the City. The location of the video monitoring systems were chosen due to documented incidents of concern to our citizens. priorDecision.heading: Plan event security within the City-property event process
priorDecision.body: Victoria’s 2025 Special Event Guidelines include a dedicated safety and security section and distinguish event personnel, police, fire and first-aid considerations. They concern events taking place on City property, not routine staffing at every private building. Use that event scope to prepare a site plan showing entrances, public circulation and emergency access, then document who coordinates security decisions and communications during setup, operation and cleanup. Review the actual security provisions with the event contact before deciding staffing or post locations. The existence of guidelines does not establish a mandatory guard count, authorize a particular contractor or demonstrate that an event permit has been approved.
